options.text: Select $400$ more residents at random and again use only the answers of those who choose to respond.

options.text: Replace each resident that did not respond with a volunteer who asks to take part.
options.why: Volunteers differ from the selected individuals in ways that can bias the results, so replacing nonrespondents with volunteers adds bias.

options.text: Contact many of the residents that did not respond again, for example by telephone or a visit, and use their answers as well.
options.why: Nonresponse bias arises because those who do not respond can differ from those who respond, so the way to reduce it is to obtain answers from as many of the selected individuals as possible.

payload.stem: A least-squares regression line is used to predict fuel economy from its weight. For a car in the data set, the residual is $-3.6$ miles per gallon. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this residual?

options.text: The actual fuel economy of a car was $3.6$ miles per gallon below the fuel economy that the line predicts for its weight.
options.why: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value, so its sign shows whether the actual value is below or above the prediction and its size shows by how much.

options.text: The line is wrong by $3.6\%$ for a car.
options.why: Treats the residual as a percent error, but a residual is measured in the units of the response variable.

options.text: The slope of the line is $-3.6$, which is the change in fuel economy for each additional unit of its weight.
options.why: Confuses the residual with the slope; the slope describes the change in the predicted value per unit of $x$.

options.text: The line predicts a fuel economy that is $3.6$ miles per gallon below the actual fuel economy of a car.
options.why: Reverses the roles of the actual and the predicted values: a residual is the actual value minus the predicted value.

parts.model_answer: Make a separate list of the renters and a separate list of the homeowners. Within each list, use a random number generator (or draw names at random) to select $50$ different residents; the two selections together form the stratified random sample.

Using the unrounded coefficients, the prediction at x = 11 is about 0.54 and the residual at x = 3 is about -0.46, so the rounding effect appears small. The rubric has no tolerance (numeric_tolerance is null), so a student who uses the unrounded line and gets, for example, -0.4617 or 0.5385 is not covered.

Rows that cannot be scored as written:
- D2 ("names both variables") has required element "in context", which is vague.
- B2 bundles units, context and the word "predicted", which are three separate ideas in one point.
- E2 requires both the word "extrapolation" and the phrase "outside the range of the data", which is over-prescriptive for a meaning-based explanation.
- Part E is labeled skill 4.D, but E1 is a pure calculation.

Part D also leaves the question of whether "explained by the linear relationship" must mention the word "linear".

payload.title: Comparing the mean score on a final exam of two independent groups

stimulus.description: A teacher wants to know whether the new method gives a higher mean exam score than the standard method. Independent random samples were taken: $34$ students of the new method had a mean score on a final exam of $81.2$ points with a standard deviation of $11.7$ points, and $35$ students of the standard method had a mean score on a final exam of $74$ points with a standard deviation of $10.3$ points. Boxplots of the two samples are roughly symmetric with no outliers. Each sample is less than $10\%$ of its population. Use a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for the test. Define any parameters you use.
parts.model_answer: Let $\mu_1$ be the mean score on a final exam for all students of the new method, and $\mu_2$ the mean for the standard method. $H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0$.

payload.stem: A random sample of $500$ voters is used to find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all voters who support a proposal. The sample proportion is $0.52$, and the conditions for inference are met. The interval is $(0.476,\ 0.564)$. Does the interval provide convincing evidence for the claim that a majority of all voters support the proposal?

options.text: Yes, because the sample proportion $0.52$ is greater than $0.5$.
options.why: Judges the claim from the sample proportion alone; the interval shows how far the population proportion can be from the sample proportion.

options.text: No, because the interval $(0.476,\ 0.564)$ includes values on both sides of $0.5$, so $0.5$ is a plausible value.
options.why: An interval that includes the value leaves it plausible, so the claim that the proportion is greater than that value is not supported.

options.text: Yes, because most of the values in the interval $(0.476,\ 0.564)$ are greater than $0.5$.
options.why: The claim is justified only if all of the plausible values satisfy it; most of them is not enough.

options.text: Yes, because a $95\%$ interval always provides convincing evidence for a claim about a proportion.
options.why: An interval supports a claim only when the value in the claim is not a plausible value; the confidence level alone does not decide this.

options.why: An interval is not required to be centered at the value in the claim; what matters is whether the value is inside the interval.

payload.stem: A least-squares regression line for predicting the number of cups of hot chocolate sold from the temperature, in degrees Celsius is $\hat y = 94.5 - 3.84x$, based on data for which $x$ ranges from $0$ to $15$, with $r = -0.91$. A researcher uses the line to predict number of cups when $x = 34$. Which of the following statements about the prediction is correct?

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is reliable, because the correlation of $0.91$ is close to $1$.
options.why: A strong correlation within the range of the data does not make predictions outside that range reliable.

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is an extrapolation, because $34$ is outside the range of the data, so the linear pattern may not continue and the prediction may be unreliable.
options.why: Predictions for values of the explanatory variable outside the range of the data assume that the linear pattern continues, which the data cannot confirm.

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is reliable, because the line is the least-squares line, which has the smallest sum of squared residuals.
options.why: The least-squares property describes the fit to the observed data, not the behavior of the relationship outside the data.

options.text: The prediction cannot be made, because a regression line can only be used for the values of $x$ that appear in the data set.
options.why: A prediction can be calculated for any value of $x$; the issue is that it is unreliable outside the range of the data.

payload.title: A stratified sample survey of students at a high school

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A researcher at a high school plans a new survey and wants to select a stratified random sample of $100$ students, with $50$ from each of two groups: freshmen and seniors. Describe how the researcher could select such a sample.
parts.model_answer: Make a separate list of the freshmen and a separate list of the seniors. Within each list, use a random number generator (or draw names at random) to select $50$ different students; the two selections together form the stratified random sample.

chooses by convenience within a group

parts.label: B

payload.title: A stratified sample survey of residents at a city
